solutions.text: PHẦN A — Đáp án

1. The government has imposed strict censorship to stop journalists reporting on the scandal. --- CENSORSHIP (noun) = sự kiểm duyệt; collocation thường gặp: "impose/strict/internet censorship". Phân biệt với "censure" (khiển trách).

2. Some newspapers resort to sensationalism, exaggerating crime stories just to attract more readers. --- SENSATIONALISM (noun, không đếm được) = lối làm tin giật gân, thổi phồng để câu khách; collocation: "tabloid/media sensationalism", "resort to sensationalism".

3. Misinformation about the vaccine spread across social media within hours. --- MISINFORMATION (noun) = thông tin sai lệch (không cố ý lừa dối); collocation: "spread/combat misinformation". Phân biệt với "disinformation" (bịa đặt có chủ đích).

4. Many young people are trapped in an echo chamber, only seeing opinions online that match what they already believe. --- ECHO CHAMBER (noun) = vòng lặp tư tưởng, chỉ tiếp xúc quan điểm củng cố niềm tin sẵn có; collocation: "trapped in/create an echo chamber".

5. That headline was clearly written as clickbait to trick people into clicking on it. --- CLICKBAIT (noun, không đếm được) = tiêu đề giật gân câu view; collocation: "clickbait headlines", "avoid/pure clickbait".

6. The football star signed an endorsement deal worth a huge sum to promote the sportswear brand. --- ENDORSEMENT (noun) = sự chứng thực/quảng bá công khai (thường có hợp đồng, trả tiền); collocation: "celebrity endorsement", "sign an endorsement deal".

7. Researchers claim that some adverts use subliminal messaging that affects our minds without us realising it. --- SUBLIMINAL (adjective) = thuộc tiềm thức, tác động dưới ngưỡng nhận thức; collocation: "subliminal advertising/messaging". Phân biệt với "subtle" (tinh tế nhưng vẫn nhận ra được).

8. The smartphone market has become so saturated with similar products that new brands struggle to compete. --- SATURATED (adjective) = bão hoà (thị trường quá đầy một loại sản phẩm); collocation cố định: "saturated WITH sth" (không dùng "by").

9. Advertisers often rely on psychological manipulation to persuade us to buy things we don't need. --- MANIPULATION (noun) = sự thao túng tâm lý/hành vi có chủ đích, luôn mang hàm ý tiêu cực; collocation: "psychological/emotional manipulation", "resist manipulation".

10. During the war, the government used propaganda broadcasts to control public opinion. --- PROPAGANDA (noun, không đếm được) = tuyên truyền (thông tin thiên lệch phục vụ mục đích chính trị); collocation: "state/political propaganda", "propaganda campaign".

11. Advertising has become so pervasive that it is almost impossible to avoid. --- PERVASIVE (adjective) = lan tràn, hiện diện khắp nơi; collocation: "pervasive advertising/influence". Phân biệt với "persuasive" (có sức thuyết phục) — hai từ dễ đọc nhầm.

12. Several shopping websites use dark patterns to make it hard for users to cancel a subscription. --- DARK PATTERNS (noun, thường ở số nhiều) = thủ thuật thiết kế giao diện nhằm đánh lừa/ép buộc người dùng; collocation: "catalogue/detect dark patterns", "dark patterns in UX design".
PHẦN B — Đáp án mẫu

1. Band 6: Adverts on social media are often designed to make young people spend money. Band 7: Social media advertisements are frequently engineered to encourage young people to spend money they may not have. Band 8: Social media advertising is meticulously engineered as a form of persuasion architecture, nudging financially inexperienced young users towards impulsive spending.

2. Band 6: Some influencers do not tell their followers when a post is an advert. Band 7: Some influencers fail to disclose to their followers when a post is actually a paid advertisement. Band 8: A considerable proportion of influencers deliberately blur the line between genuine recommendation and paid endorsement, exploiting the parasocial trust they have cultivated with their followers.

3. Band 6: People believe fake news because it spreads faster than real news. Band 7: People often believe fake news simply because misinformation tends to spread more quickly than accurate reporting. Band 8: Disinformation frequently gains significant traction precisely because sensational falsehoods propagate far more rapidly than sober, fact-checked journalism.

4. Band 6: Companies use famous people in adverts because people trust them. Band 7: Companies feature celebrities in their advertisements because consumers tend to trust well-known public figures. Band 8: Brands routinely secure celebrity endorsements in order to confer instant credibility on an otherwise unremarkable product.

5. Band 6: Newspapers sometimes make stories more exciting than they really are. Band 7: Newspapers sometimes exaggerate stories to make them seem more exciting than they actually are. Band 8: Certain publications resort to sensationalism, distorting the facts of a story at the expense of accurate, balanced reporting.

6. Band 6: It is hard to stop children from seeing adverts for unhealthy food. Band 7: It is difficult to prevent children from being exposed to advertisements for unhealthy food. Band 8: Given how pervasive digital marketing has become, shielding children from advertisements for unhealthy food has proved an almost insurmountable challenge.

7. Band 6: Websites use tricks to make people agree to things they don't really want. Band 7: Websites use manipulative design tricks to pressure people into agreeing to things they don't really want. Band 8: Numerous websites deploy dark patterns, such as confirmshaming, to coerce users into consenting to options they would not otherwise choose.

8. Band 6: Governments should make stricter rules about political adverts online. Band 7: Governments should introduce stricter regulations governing political advertisements online. Band 8: Given the scale of micro-targeted political advertising, governments would do well to impose far stricter regulation, including mandatory transparency registers and spending caps.

passages.text: For most of the twentieth century, the boundary between editorial content and paid persuasion was, at least in principle, plainly marked: advertisements occupied paid columns, sponsored segments carried disclosure language, and trust in journalistic institutions depended in part on the visibility of that boundary. A more recent generation of media researchers has begun to argue, in the writer's view persuasively, that the boundary has been quietly eroded by two practices: native advertising and surveillance-based targeting. The story matters because the institutions designed to police misleading commercial speech were calibrated around an older media architecture.

The case for taking native advertising seriously as a regulatory problem rests, in the first place, on its measured invisibility. According to Professor Helena Vasquez, a media economist at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, the controlled experiments her group has run with roughly four thousand five hundred participants in seven countries indicate that approximately forty-one per cent of readers do not recognise clearly labelled native articles as commercial in nature, even when the disclosure text appears at the top of the page. Vasquez's argument is that the persistent recognition gap is not a marginal design flaw but a structural feature of formats designed to blend into surrounding editorial copy. Disclosure as currently practised, on her reading, does not perform the work that consumer-protection law assumes it performs.

The surveillance dimension is no less interesting. A 2023 audit commissioned by an inter-governmental research group examined the data flows associated with three thousand and forty-eight commercial websites and reported that, on average, each visit triggered requests to roughly thirty-one third-party domains, including data brokers and behavioural-targeting services. Vasquez cautions that "third party" is doing considerable work in the sentence, since many of those domains belong to integrated networks rather than independent actors. The headline figure nevertheless suggests that the data infrastructure now underpinning routine browsing is substantially denser than most users assume, and that the consent forms which mediate this infrastructure provide, in her view, a thin form of authorisation at best.

The first sustained critique of the "quiet erosion" framing has come from Professor Cyrus Avanesian, a marketing scholar at the Wharton School in Pennsylvania. Avanesian concedes that recognition gaps and dense data flows are real, but resists the idea that they amount to a structural failure of consumer protection. Markets, he argues, contain self-correcting mechanisms: advertisers who lean too heavily on disguised formats face reputational costs when investigative journalists expose the practice, and platforms have a long-term interest in maintaining the trust on which advertising revenue ultimately depends. Avanesian's group has reviewed twenty-three legal cases in which disguised native campaigns produced measurable reputational damage to the advertising brand, and his interpretation is that the boundary, while imperfect, is policed in practice by ordinary commercial pressures rather than by regulation alone.

These two views are not in direct conflict, but they pull policy attention in different directions. If the central problem is the structural invisibility of formats designed to bypass critical attention, then the appropriate response involves stricter disclosure standards, mandatory format conventions and, possibly, restrictions on how editorial and advertising teams may share infrastructure. If, on the other hand, the central problem is the slower correction of occasional excesses by competitive markets, then the appropriate response involves transparency requirements, ex-post enforcement and, in extreme cases, antitrust action against dominant platforms. Both interpretations would, in principle, accommodate the same recognition-gap and data-flow figures, although they disagree on which lever most urgently requires attention.

A separate strand of research has focused on the experience of audiences themselves. Researchers in media psychology, including Professor Joon-sang Kim of Yonsei University in Seoul, have argued that the more interesting effect of native and surveillance-based formats may not be the direct change in purchasing behaviour but the slow erosion of the user's sense of being addressed honestly. In repeated qualitative studies with roughly six hundred participants, Kim's group has traced how everyday browsers, when shown the data trails generated by their own visits to common news sites, describe a creeping mistrust that extends beyond the advertisements themselves to the surrounding editorial content. The drift of a single browsing session through a network of unrelated third parties, she argues, is a quiet revolution in the everyday experience of reading the news, and one which the more conventional debate over disclosure tends to overlook.

The most interesting recent work has shifted from whether the boundary has been eroded to what would be required to restore it. The legal forms developed in the twentieth century — clearly labelled advertorials, mandatory disclosure boxes, separation between editorial and commercial sales teams — were designed for an architecture in which the carrier of the message and the targeting of the audience were comparatively separable. Once targeting depends on real-time auctions over user attributes, those forms may need to be redesigned rather than simply enforced. Some commentators argue that the existing law is adequate if enforced more strictly. Others point out that adequate enforcement against a moving target may itself require redesigning the categories that the law uses.

The fairest assessment lies somewhere in the middle of these claims. The current ecosystem is neither a wholesale collapse of editorial integrity nor a routine extension of older marketing practice. It is an unusually opaque case of regulatory mismatch that contains many of the tensions that still trouble media policy: the relationship between disclosure and design, between consent and infrastructure, between market discipline and individual cognitive load. Reading the present moment with these tensions in mind is more useful than treating it as either a familiar marketing question or an unprecedented crisis.

What current research does support is the modest claim that the boundary between editorial content and paid persuasion is now substantially less visible to ordinary readers than the legal architecture assumes, and that any account of contemporary media regulation that ignores this gap is unlikely to age well.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture extends our media-economics research strand to the empirical literature on so-called "native advertising" — commercial content engineered to mimic the editorial style of the platform on which it appears — and audiences' diminishing ability to detect it. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Anastasia Vukotic-Lindqvist — that's V-U-K-O-T-I-C hyphen L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T; one hyphen, and note the Q is followed by V, not U, in the Swedish portion. So Vukotic-Lindqvist. Her 2017 monograph reframed sponsored-content analysis away from a deception-binary lens into what she calls "persuasion-recognition latency". [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Vukotic-Lindqvist's framework USED TO be operationalised through post-exposure recognition questionnaires only, NOW the field deploys triangulated mixed-methods designs incorporating eye-tracking dwell-time data, click-path telemetry, and think-aloud transcripts, and from 2028 a multi-platform consortium WILL be rolling out neurometric attention modules. Past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, the eye-tracking mixed-methods phase. [pause:3s] The longitudinal cohort I want to reference today was first surveyed in 2020 — sorry, let me correct that, 2019; the published descriptive statistics in 2020 covered baseline data collected in 2019. So whenever I refer to the baseline year for the Helsinki audience cohort, please record 2019. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The construct Vukotic-Lindqvist foregrounds — the measurable interval between a reader's first contact with sponsored content and their conscious tagging of it as commercial — is termed "persuasion-recognition latency". You'll encounter related labels in the older literature: ad-detection lag, sponsorship blindness, editorial-camouflage delay. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Vukotic-Lindqvist's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is persuasion-recognition latency — p-e-r-s-u-a-s-i-o-n hyphen recognition latency. So when the older literature uses ad-detection lag or sponsorship blindness, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what media economists call the "disclosure-salience continuum". When ethnographers describe how readers process disclosure labels embedded in native content, they sketch a graded continuum running from overt-salient labelling through ambient-peripheral labelling to camouflage-equivalent labelling. So, you know, you'll see articles tagged "PAID PARTNERSHIP" in bold yellow at the top — that's overt-salient. Or articles, kinda, marked with a small grey "sponsored" tag tucked into the by-line — that's camouflage-equivalent. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the disclosure-salience continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the survey data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the seven hundred and twenty adults we tested across three platforms last quarter, MOST failed to identify the sponsored article within thirty seconds — roughly seventy-one per cent. Only a few — about nine per cent — identified it almost immediately, and some — twenty per cent — needed prompted disclosure cues before tagging. So delayed-recognition dominates numerically, but the nine-per-cent fast-detector tail, though small, is theoretically significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "trust transfer". This refers to a temporal pattern in which credibility cues from the surrounding editorial environment leak across to the sponsored item, inflating perceived neutrality. At the Helsinki test site, our analysts documented one hundred and forty-six trust-transfer events across the cohort during one twelve-week window. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that clearer disclosure labels linearly reduce persuasion impact is, frankly, not supported. Most of the readers in our sample did NOT exhibit the predicted monotonic drop in purchase intent as label prominence increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a flat or even slightly U-shaped response, suggesting that disclosure alone is an insufficient countermeasure. So the older "disclosure-equals-immunity" hypothesis, which predicts linear reduction, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT eye-tracking mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in this afternoon's seminar. I want you to focus on the dwell-time protocols specifically, not the neurometric futures or the legacy questionnaire instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: native advertising outcomes are best understood through persuasion-recognition latency, not the deception binary; the technical term for the recognition interval is persuasion-recognition latency; delayed recognition dominates at roughly seventy-one per cent; and the disclosure-equals-immunity hypothesis is not empirically supported in this cohort. Next week we'll examine platform-recommender economics. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: Modern marketing has evolved far beyond the printed billboard, deploying psychological insights and personalised algorithms to influence behaviour in subtle ways. Some commentators therefore claim that today's consumers can no longer make genuinely free choices. While I partially agree, I would argue the truth lies somewhere in the middle: advertising is undeniably manipulative, yet most consumers still retain meaningful agency.

Those who hold the stronger view raise legitimate concerns. Targeted ads, fuelled by vast troves of behavioural data, now anticipate desires before consumers consciously feel them. It is the precision of these algorithms that makes them so unsettling: a brief pause on a video can trigger weeks of tailored prompts. Furthermore, techniques such as sensationalism, subliminal cues and influencer endorsements blur the line between editorial content and paid promotion, which tends to undermine informed decision-making. Children in particular, who lack mature critical faculties, may indeed have little real choice.

Nevertheless, the claim that all adult consumers are essentially powerless seems overstated. People remain capable of comparing prices, reading independent reviews and ignoring intrusive pop-ups. Regulatory bodies in many jurisdictions now require disclosure of sponsored content, and media-literacy programmes are slowly expanding. What also matters is the rise of consumer activism: boycotts and online callouts have forced major brands to abandon misleading campaigns, which suggests that the audience is far from passive.

In conclusion, I agree that manipulation has reached unprecedented levels, especially for vulnerable groups, yet I disagree that genuine choice has been abolished. What citizens require is stronger regulation of data-driven targeting and broader media-literacy education. With these safeguards, consumers can continue to navigate the advertising-saturated landscape with reasonable, if imperfect, autonomy.

That contemporary advertising leans heavily on behavioural science is beyond dispute; whether it has eroded consumer autonomy to the point of abolishing free choice is a much stronger claim. Having weighed the evidence, I partially agree: the architecture of modern persuasion has unquestionably narrowed the space for unmediated decision-making, yet to deny consumers any agency at all overstates the case.

Proponents of the strong thesis advance powerful arguments. Surveillance-grade tracking now feeds machine-learning systems that micro-target individuals at moments of maximal susceptibility. What such platforms have engineered is, in effect, a closed loop of dark patterns, scarcity nudges and parasocial endorsements that bypass deliberation altogether. So sophisticated has algorithmic curation become that users frequently mistake commercially incentivised suggestions for their own preferences. For children and digitally inexperienced adults, the asymmetry between consumer and advertiser arguably approximates coercion.

However, treating consumers as wholly captive understates several countervailing forces. Regulatory regimes, from the EU's Digital Services Act to advertising-standards authorities elsewhere, are gradually mandating disclosure, banning manipulative interface designs and limiting the profiling of minors. Equally important is the emergence of media-literacy curricula, which appear to inoculate younger cohorts against sensationalism and clickbait. Furthermore, consumer activism - viral boycotts, brand-accountability campaigns, transparency dashboards - increasingly disciplines advertisers who overstep ethical norms. Nor should the rise of ad-free subscription models be ignored; they demonstrate that demand for less manipulative environments is itself a commercial force.

On balance, then, I align with a moderated version of the proposition. What modern advertising has eroded is not choice per se but the cognitive conditions under which choice is exercised. The appropriate response is stronger fiduciary obligations on platforms, robust media-literacy education and enforceable design standards - not resignation to determinism.

solutions.text: PHẦN A — Đáp án

1. The government has imposed strict censorship to stop journalists reporting on the scandal. --- CENSORSHIP (noun) = sự kiểm duyệt; collocation thường gặp: "impose/strict/internet censorship". Phân biệt với "censure" (khiển trách).

2. Some newspapers resort to sensationalism, exaggerating crime stories just to attract more readers. --- SENSATIONALISM (noun, không đếm được) = lối làm tin giật gân, thổi phồng để câu khách; collocation: "tabloid/media sensationalism", "resort to sensationalism".

3. Misinformation about the vaccine spread across social media within hours. --- MISINFORMATION (noun) = thông tin sai lệch (không cố ý lừa dối); collocation: "spread/combat misinformation". Phân biệt với "disinformation" (bịa đặt có chủ đích).

4. Many young people are trapped in an echo chamber, only seeing opinions online that match what they already believe. --- ECHO CHAMBER (noun) = vòng lặp tư tưởng, chỉ tiếp xúc quan điểm củng cố niềm tin sẵn có; collocation: "trapped in/create an echo chamber".

5. That headline was clearly written as clickbait to trick people into clicking on it. --- CLICKBAIT (noun, không đếm được) = tiêu đề giật gân câu view; collocation: "clickbait headlines", "avoid/pure clickbait".

6. The football star signed an endorsement deal worth a huge sum to promote the sportswear brand. --- ENDORSEMENT (noun) = sự chứng thực/quảng bá công khai (thường có hợp đồng, trả tiền); collocation: "celebrity endorsement", "sign an endorsement deal".

7. Researchers claim that some adverts use subliminal messaging that affects our minds without us realising it. --- SUBLIMINAL (adjective) = thuộc tiềm thức, tác động dưới ngưỡng nhận thức; collocation: "subliminal advertising/messaging". Phân biệt với "subtle" (tinh tế nhưng vẫn nhận ra được).

8. The smartphone market has become so saturated with similar products that new brands struggle to compete. --- SATURATED (adjective) = bão hoà (thị trường quá đầy một loại sản phẩm); collocation cố định: "saturated WITH sth" (không dùng "by").

9. Advertisers often rely on psychological manipulation to persuade us to buy things we don't need. --- MANIPULATION (noun) = sự thao túng tâm lý/hành vi có chủ đích, luôn mang hàm ý tiêu cực; collocation: "psychological/emotional manipulation", "resist manipulation".

10. During the war, the government used propaganda broadcasts to control public opinion. --- PROPAGANDA (noun, không đếm được) = tuyên truyền (thông tin thiên lệch phục vụ mục đích chính trị); collocation: "state/political propaganda", "propaganda campaign".

11. Advertising has become so pervasive that it is almost impossible to avoid. --- PERVASIVE (adjective) = lan tràn, hiện diện khắp nơi; collocation: "pervasive advertising/influence". Phân biệt với "persuasive" (có sức thuyết phục) — hai từ dễ đọc nhầm.

12. Several shopping websites use dark patterns to make it hard for users to cancel a subscription. --- DARK PATTERNS (noun, thường ở số nhiều) = thủ thuật thiết kế giao diện nhằm đánh lừa/ép buộc người dùng; collocation: "catalogue/detect dark patterns", "dark patterns in UX design".
PHẦN B — Đáp án mẫu

1. Band 6: Adverts on social media are often designed to make young people spend money. Band 7: Social media advertisements are frequently engineered to encourage young people to spend money they may not have. Band 8: Social media advertising is meticulously engineered as a form of persuasion architecture, nudging financially inexperienced young users towards impulsive spending.

2. Band 6: Some influencers do not tell their followers when a post is an advert. Band 7: Some influencers fail to disclose to their followers when a post is actually a paid advertisement. Band 8: A considerable proportion of influencers deliberately blur the line between genuine recommendation and paid endorsement, exploiting the parasocial trust they have cultivated with their followers.

3. Band 6: People believe fake news because it spreads faster than real news. Band 7: People often believe fake news simply because misinformation tends to spread more quickly than accurate reporting. Band 8: Disinformation frequently gains significant traction precisely because sensational falsehoods propagate far more rapidly than sober, fact-checked journalism.

4. Band 6: Companies use famous people in adverts because people trust them. Band 7: Companies feature celebrities in their advertisements because consumers tend to trust well-known public figures. Band 8: Brands routinely secure celebrity endorsements in order to confer instant credibility on an otherwise unremarkable product.

5. Band 6: Newspapers sometimes make stories more exciting than they really are. Band 7: Newspapers sometimes exaggerate stories to make them seem more exciting than they actually are. Band 8: Certain publications resort to sensationalism, distorting the facts of a story at the expense of accurate, balanced reporting.

6. Band 6: It is hard to stop children from seeing adverts for unhealthy food. Band 7: It is difficult to prevent children from being exposed to advertisements for unhealthy food. Band 8: Given how pervasive digital marketing has become, shielding children from advertisements for unhealthy food has proved an almost insurmountable challenge.

7. Band 6: Websites use tricks to make people agree to things they don't really want. Band 7: Websites use manipulative design tricks to pressure people into agreeing to things they don't really want. Band 8: Numerous websites deploy dark patterns, such as confirmshaming, to coerce users into consenting to options they would not otherwise choose.

8. Band 6: Governments should make stricter rules about political adverts online. Band 7: Governments should introduce stricter regulations governing political advertisements online. Band 8: Given the scale of micro-targeted political advertising, governments would do well to impose far stricter regulation, including mandatory transparency registers and spending caps.

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~270 words)

The advertisement I'd like to discuss is Apple's "Shot on iPhone" campaign, specifically the 2020 instalment featuring footage filmed entirely on the iPhone 11 Pro by professional cinematographers across thirty countries. I encountered it initially as a billboard during a layover at Changi Airport, then later as an Instagram series, and it ultimately nudged me into purchasing the device — despite my prior loyalty to Android.

What the campaign showed, on the surface, was a montage of breathtakingly cinematic vignettes: a Mongolian eagle hunter at dawn, fishermen casting nets off the Vietnamese coast, neon-drenched Tokyo street scenes. Crucially, none of the imagery foregrounded the product itself; the phone appeared only as a small caption acknowledging the device used. What Apple essentially deployed here was a textbook example of "persuasion architecture" — the deliberate engineering of consumer desire through aspirational identification rather than overt salesmanship.

The reasons it worked on me, despite my self-image as a critical consumer, are worth dissecting. Firstly, the campaign sidestepped traditional advertising clichés — no specs, no comparison charts — and instead positioned the iPhone as a creative instrument rather than a gadget. Secondly, the user-generated dimension created an aura of authenticity that no scripted commercial could replicate; the photographers were credited by Instagram handle, which made the marketing feel participatory.

Reflecting on it now, I recognise that the advertisement didn't really inform my decision so much as reframe my self-perception — it sold me a version of myself as a more creative, observant person. That, ultimately, is the disquieting genius of contemporary brand advertising: rarely does it sell products, and what it sells instead is identity. The phone, when I unboxed it, was almost incidental.

blocks.text: Q1: Should political advertising be regulated?

Point: Yes, decisively — political advertising, particularly the micro-targeted variety that proliferates on social platforms, ought to be subject to far stricter regulation than the current laissez-faire approach permits.

Explain: The core issue is that political ads operate in a fundamentally different epistemic environment than commercial ones: they shape voting behaviour and democratic legitimacy, yet platforms allow advertisers to target tiny demographic slivers with bespoke messages that escape public scrutiny. What this enables is precisely the kind of disinformation arbitrage that erodes informed consent.

Example: The Cambridge Analytica scandal in 2018 exposed how 87 million Facebook profiles were harvested to deliver psychographically tailored political messaging during the Brexit referendum and US presidential election — a textbook abuse of persuasion architecture. The EU's Digital Services Act, which came into force in 2024, now mandates transparency registers for political ads, requiring disclosure of funding and targeting parameters. Singapore goes further, banning foreign political advertising outright.
Link: So while outright bans are heavy-handed, mandatory transparency, spending caps, and bans on micro-targeting strike a reasonable balance between free expression and democratic integrity.
Q2: Are influencers ethical advertisers?

Point: The ethics of influencer marketing are, in my view, genuinely fraught — and while a minority of creators maintain credible editorial standards, the sector as a whole leans towards practices that I'd characterise as deceptive by design.

Explain: The fundamental issue is the deliberate blurring of personal recommendation and paid endorsement: influencers cultivate parasocial trust precisely so they can monetise it, and the resulting content exploits cognitive biases that traditional advertising disclosure rules were never designed to address. Younger audiences, in particular, struggle to distinguish authentic content from sponsored material.

Example: Regulatory reviews of influencer marketing have found that a significant proportion of posts violate disclosure requirements, with fashion and supplement categories being among the worst offenders. The Kim Kardashian SEC fine of $1.26 million for promoting an unregistered crypto token illustrated how influence-as-advertising can shade into outright fraud. Conversely, creators on platforms like Substack, who openly disclose conflicts and refuse sponsorships, demonstrate that ethical models are possible — just rarely profitable.

Link: So while regulation is catching up, the sector's structural incentives push towards opacity, and consumers are well-advised to treat influencer recommendations with the same scepticism reserved for billboard advertising.
Q3: Does advertising create needs?

Point: I'd argue that advertising doesn't strictly create needs from scratch — that's an overstatement of its power — but it absolutely manufactures wants and amplifies anxieties in ways that distort genuine welfare.

Explain: The fundamental insight, drawn from economists like Galbraith, is that production in modern economies has so vastly outstripped basic subsistence requirements that demand itself has to be engineered through what he called the "dependence effect." Advertising channels biological drives — for status, belonging, security — onto specific commodified solutions.

Example: The deodorant industry is perhaps the canonical illustration: prior to Listerine's 1920s campaign popularising the term "halitosis," bad breath simply wasn't a culturally salient anxiety. Today, the global personal care market exceeds $500 billion annually, largely built on insecurities that previous generations didn't recognise as problems. Similarly, the diamond engagement ring tradition was almost single-handedly manufactured by De Beers' 1947 "A Diamond is Forever" campaign.
Link: So while advertising can't conjure needs ex nihilo, its capacity to redefine social norms and weaponise insecurity is significant — and worth treating with informed scepticism.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good morning. Today's lecture dissects three concepts that, properly understood, expose the commercial architecture of the digital sphere: persuasion architecture, dark patterns and the attention economy. The illusion that platforms are passive conduits is, frankly, untenable.

> Let us begin with persuasion architecture, a term coined by the technology ethicist Zeynep Tufekci. Tufekci's contention is that digital interfaces are meticulously engineered to nudge — every shade of blue, every haptic buzz, every infinite-scroll feed has been A/B-tested to maximise time-on-platform. The principles draw on the behavioural-economics insights of Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, but, importantly, repurposed for commercial extraction rather than welfare.

> Now, dark patterns. The user-experience researcher Harry Brignull catalogued these in 2010 — interfaces that misdirect, shame, or coerce the user. Familiar examples include the roach motel (easy to subscribe, near-impossible to cancel), the confirmshaming prompt ("No thanks, I don't want to save money"), and disguised advertising masquerading as editorial content. A 2022 audit by the European Commission found dark patterns on ninety-seven percent of the major e-commerce sites surveyed.

> Finally, the attention economy. The thesis, advanced by the late Herbert Simon as early as 1971, holds that in an information-rich world, attention itself becomes the scarce resource. Contemporary platforms — TikTok, YouTube, Instagram — monetise that scarcity through algorithmic amplification of emotionally provocative content. Engagement metrics reward outrage and dread; calm deliberation rarely goes viral.

Now, that engagement-versus-wellbeing curve on table four is sobering, but I want to push past mere description and ask a harder question — what happens when the persuasion machinery is fused with the recommendation engine? Because the truly modern development is not that platforms grab attention; it is that they learn, in real time, exactly which lever works on you specifically. This is what some scholars call hypernudging — personalised, dynamic, continuously updated manipulation. [pause] A static billboard nudges everyone identically; an algorithmic feed nudges each user along a bespoke trajectory, recalibrated with every swipe.

Consider the documented dynamic of the so-called rabbit hole. Investigations into recommendation systems — including the Mozilla Foundation's crowdsourced YouTube study — found that the algorithm reliably escalates: a viewer who pauses on mildly provocative content is steered toward progressively more extreme material, because extremity sustains engagement. The system is not malicious; it is, um, simply optimising the metric it was given. And that is precisely the danger. There is no villain in the loop, only an objective function indifferent to anything but watch-time.

Let me add a sharper edge from developmental psychology. The adolescent brain, with its still-maturing prefrontal cortex, is constitutionally more sensitive to variable social reward — the unpredictable trickle of likes that mimics, quite deliberately, the reinforcement schedule of a slot machine. Tristan Harris has been blunt about this: features such as pull-to-refresh borrow directly from the design grammar of gambling. [pause] When you engineer a near-miss into a notification feed, you are not nudging; you are conditioning.

So the picture darkens from the one I sketched earlier. It is not simply that calm deliberation fails to go viral — it is that the architecture is actively training a generation away from it, one optimised micro-interaction at a time. Which is why the regulatory question we turn to next cannot stop at transparency, but must instead ask whether…

> The synthesis is bleak: when persuasion architecture, dark patterns and attention monetisation converge, user agency is the casualty. Regulation lags, predictably, two decades behind the technology. Now, please look at table four, which maps engagement-versus-wellbeing curves…

•  Chọn 'mỏ neo' Overview (45s): kênh nào dẫn đầu cả hai panel (social media) và kênh nào đội sổ cả hai (print) làm luận điểm tổng quan.
•  Gom kênh thành cụm (30s): digital dẫn đầu (social, display) / truyền thống đội sổ (print, radio) / television trung gian.
•  Viết thân bài theo panel: đoạn 2 ad spend với so sánh bội số, đoạn 3 audience reach + một câu liên panel.
•  Kết bằng suy luận xuyên panel (chi tiêu bám theo độ phủ khán giả); tuyệt đối khớp từng con số với dữ liệu.
T17 — ADVERTISING & MEDIA · Writing Task 2
(1) Đề bài
Đề bài.  Manipulation in advertising has become so sophisticated that consumers can no longer make truly free choices. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
(2) Từ vựng chủ đề (Band 8 topic & argument lexis)

Vast troves of behavioural data feed the algorithms that micro-target users.

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
Phía đồng tình (lựa chọn đã bị xói mòn):
•  Quảng cáo nhắm mục tiêu dựa trên dữ liệu hành vi đoán trước ham muốn, micro-target đúng thời điểm dễ tổn thương nhất.
•  Dark patterns, tín hiệu tiềm thức và influencer endorsement vượt qua suy xét lý trí, làm mờ ranh giới nội dung và quảng cáo.
•  Trẻ em và người ít kinh nghiệm số thiếu năng lực phản biện nên gần như không có lựa chọn thực sự.
Phía phản biện (người tiêu dùng vẫn còn quyền tự quyết):
•  Người dùng vẫn so giá, đọc đánh giá độc lập, bỏ qua pop-up và chặn quảng cáo.
•  Quy định (Digital Services Act, cơ quan chuẩn quảng cáo) buộc công khai nội dung tài trợ và cấm thiết kế đánh lừa.
•  Consumer activism (tẩy chay, gọi tên trực tuyến) và mô hình thuê bao không quảng cáo cho thấy người dùng không thụ động.
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion
•  Introduction — diễn giải tranh luận; luận điểm: thao túng đã đạt mức chưa từng có nhưng chưa xoá bỏ hoàn toàn quyền lựa chọn.
•  Body 1 — phía đồng tình: dữ liệu hành vi + dark patterns + influencer thu hẹp không gian quyết định, nhất là với nhóm dễ tổn thương.
•  Body 2 — phía phản biện: năng lực truyền thông, quy định và vận động tiêu dùng giúp người dùng giữ quyền tự quyết.
•  Conclusion — đồng tình một phần: cần quy định data-targeting mạnh hơn và giáo dục media literacy, không phải đầu hàng thuyết định mệnh.
(5) Mẫu câu luyện tập (Practice sentences)

What such platforms have engineered is, in effect, a closed loop of dark patterns and parasocial endorsements that bypass deliberation.

rows: "persuasion now permeates every digital touchpoint consumers encounter"
"micro-targeting exploits cognitive biases at moments of maximal susceptibility"

"commercial incentives increasingly dictate which products ever reach the consumer's attention"

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~273 words)

Modern marketing has evolved far beyond the printed billboard, deploying psychological insights and personalised algorithms to influence behaviour in subtle ways. Some commentators therefore claim that today's consumers can no longer make genuinely free choices. While I partially agree, I would argue the truth lies somewhere in the middle: advertising is undeniably manipulative, yet most consumers still retain meaningful agency.

Those who hold the stronger view raise legitimate concerns. Targeted ads, fuelled by vast troves of behavioural data, now anticipate desires before consumers consciously feel them. It is the precision of these algorithms that makes them so unsettling: a brief pause on a video can trigger weeks of tailored prompts. Furthermore, techniques such as sensationalism, subliminal cues and influencer endorsements blur the line between editorial content and paid promotion, which tends to undermine informed decision-making. Children in particular, who lack mature critical faculties, may indeed have little real choice.

Nevertheless, the claim that all adult consumers are essentially powerless seems overstated. People remain capable of comparing prices, reading independent reviews and ignoring intrusive pop-ups. Regulatory bodies in many jurisdictions now require disclosure of sponsored content, and media-literacy programmes are slowly expanding. What also matters is the rise of consumer activism: boycotts and online callouts have forced major brands to abandon misleading campaigns, which suggests that the audience is far from passive.

In conclusion, I agree that manipulation has reached unprecedented levels, especially for vulnerable groups, yet I disagree that genuine choice has been abolished. What citizens require is stronger regulation of data-driven targeting and broader media-literacy education. With these safeguards, consumers can continue to navigate the advertising-saturated landscape with reasonable, if imperfect, autonomy.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~284 words)

That contemporary advertising leans heavily on behavioural science is beyond dispute; whether it has eroded consumer autonomy to the point of abolishing free choice is a much stronger claim. Having weighed the evidence, I partially agree: the architecture of modern persuasion has unquestionably narrowed the space for unmediated decision-making, yet to deny consumers any agency at all overstates the case.

Proponents of the strong thesis advance powerful arguments. Surveillance-grade tracking now feeds machine-learning systems that micro-target individuals at moments of maximal susceptibility. What such platforms have engineered is, in effect, a closed loop of dark patterns, scarcity nudges and parasocial endorsements that bypass deliberation altogether. So sophisticated has algorithmic curation become that users frequently mistake commercially incentivised suggestions for their own preferences. For children and digitally inexperienced adults, the asymmetry between consumer and advertiser arguably approximates coercion.

However, treating consumers as wholly captive understates several countervailing forces. Regulatory regimes, from the EU's Digital Services Act to advertising-standards authorities elsewhere, are gradually mandating disclosure, banning manipulative interface designs and limiting the profiling of minors. Equally important is the emergence of media-literacy curricula, which appear to inoculate younger cohorts against sensationalism and clickbait. Furthermore, consumer activism — viral boycotts, brand-accountability campaigns, transparency dashboards — increasingly disciplines advertisers who overstep ethical norms. Nor should the rise of ad-free subscription models be ignored; they demonstrate that demand for less manipulative environments is itself a commercial force.

On balance, then, I align with a moderated version of the proposition. What modern advertising has eroded is not choice per se but the cognitive conditions under which choice is exercised. The appropriate response is stronger fiduciary obligations on platforms, robust media-literacy education and enforceable design standards — not resignation to determinism.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 triển khai cú pháp cao cấp xuyên suốt (đảo ngữ 'So sophisticated has algorithmic curation become', 'Nor should the rise... be ignored'; cleft 'What such platforms have engineered is') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng vài lần.

•  Band 8 dẫn bằng chứng cụ thể, đương đại (Digital Services Act, transparency dashboards, ad-free subscription models) và lexis Band 8 ('dark patterns', 'parasocial endorsements', 'scarcity nudges', 'fiduciary obligations'), nâng Task Response và Lexical Resource một bậc.

•  Band 8 khép luận điểm bằng cleft tương phản tinh tế ('not choice per se but the cognitive conditions...') và register học thuật nhất quán, loại bỏ cụm hơi đời thường như 'online callouts' của bản 7.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The government strongly denies enforcing internet **censorship** in the country.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'censor' nghe gần 'sensor' (cảm biến) → một "bộ cảm biến" lọc bỏ thông tin không mong muốn.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'censor' (kiểm duyệt viên/kiểm duyệt - động từ) với 'censure' (khiển trách, chỉ trích).
vocabulary.definition_en: the suppression or prohibition of speech, media, or information considered politically unacceptable or harmful
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự kiểm duyệt (thông tin, truyền thông)
vocabulary.example: The government strongly denies enforcing internet censorship in the country.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'censor' nghe gần 'sensor' (cảm biến) → một 'bộ cảm biến' lọc bỏ thông tin không mong muốn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Lối làm tin giật gân, phóng đại để thu hút sự chú ý bất chấp độ chính xác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The newspaper is widely criticised for its **sensationalism** in reporting crime stories.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sensation' (cảm giác mạnh) + -alism → biến tin tức thành thứ gây "cảm giác mạnh" bất chấp sự thật.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Sensationalism' (danh từ trừu tượng, không đếm được) khác với 'sensation' (một cảm giác/sự kiện gây chấn động cụ thể, đếm được).
vocabulary.definition_en: the use of exciting, shocking, or exaggerated stories at the expense of accuracy, to provoke public interest
vocabulary.definition_vi: lối làm tin giật gân, thổi phồng để câu khách
vocabulary.example: The newspaper is widely criticised for its sensationalism in reporting crime stories.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sensation' (cảm giác mạnh) + -alism → biến tin tức thành thứ gây 'cảm giác mạnh' bất chấp sự thật.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thông tin sai lệch, thường lan truyền không có chủ đích lừa dối rõ ràng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Fake news and **misinformation** spread incredibly fast on the internet.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'mis-' (sai) + 'information' (thông tin) → thông tin bị sai lệch, dù không cố ý.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'misinformation' (sai lệch do vô ý) với 'disinformation' (bịa đặt có chủ đích để lừa dối).
vocabulary.definition_en: false or inaccurate information, especially when spread carelessly rather than with deliberate intent to deceive
vocabulary.definition_vi: thông tin sai lệch (không cố ý lừa dối)
vocabulary.example: Fake news and misinformation spread incredibly fast on the internet.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'mis-' (sai) + 'information' (thông tin) → thông tin bị sai lệch, dù không cố ý.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vòng lặp tư tưởng trên mạng, nơi người dùng chỉ thấy quan điểm củng cố niềm tin sẵn có của mình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> This phenomenon traps users in isolated **echo chambers**, reinforcing their existing biases.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'echo' (tiếng vọng) + 'chamber' (căn phòng) → một căn phòng chỉ vọng lại đúng ý kiến của chính mình.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng dạng danh từ ghép 'echo chamber', không tách nghĩa đen 'phòng vọng âm' khi nói về mạng xã hội.
vocabulary.definition_en: an online environment in which people only encounter opinions and information that reinforce their own existing beliefs
vocabulary.definition_vi: vòng lặp tư tưởng (chỉ tiếp xúc với quan điểm giống mình)
vocabulary.example: This phenomenon traps users in isolated echo chambers, reinforcing their existing biases.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'echo' (tiếng vọng) + 'chamber' (căn phòng) → một căn phòng chỉ vọng lại đúng ý kiến của chính mình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiêu đề giật gân, gây tò mò nhằm câu lượt nhấp chuột.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Writers often use **clickbait** headlines to trick users into clicking on their articles.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'click' (nhấp chuột) + 'bait' (mồi câu) → mồi câu dụ người đọc bấm vào.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Clickbait' là danh từ không đếm được, không dùng 'a clickbait' hay 'clickbaits'.
vocabulary.definition_en: web content whose main purpose is to attract attention through misleading or sensational headlines
vocabulary.definition_vi: tiêu đề câu view/câu like (nội dung giật tít gây tò mò)
vocabulary.example: Writers often use clickbait headlines to trick users into clicking on their articles.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'click' (nhấp chuột) + 'bait' (mồi câu) → mồi câu dụ người đọc bấm vào.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự chứng thực hoặc quảng bá công khai cho sản phẩm, thường bởi người nổi tiếng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The athlete signed a multi-million dollar **endorsement** deal with a famous shoe brand.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'endorse' = ký tên ủng hộ (từ 'dorsum' - lưng, mặt sau tờ séc) → công khai đứng sau ủng hộ sản phẩm.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Endorsement' (sự chứng thực công khai, có hợp đồng) khác với 'recommendation' (lời giới thiệu cá nhân, không nhất thiết trả tiền).
vocabulary.definition_en: a public expression of approval or support, especially of a product or service by a celebrity
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự chứng thực, quảng bá (thường bởi người nổi tiếng)
vocabulary.example: The athlete signed a multi-million dollar endorsement deal with a famous shoe brand.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'endorse' = ký tên ủng hộ (từ 'dorsum' - lưng, mặt sau tờ séc) → công khai đứng sau ủng hộ sản phẩm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuộc tiềm thức, tác động đến tâm trí mà con người không nhận thức được.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Some advertising messages go into your brain without you even noticing, exploiting **subliminal** cues.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sub-' (dưới) + 'limen' (ngưỡng cửa, tiếng Latin) → thông điệp nằm dưới ngưỡng nhận thức.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Subliminal' mô tả thông điệp dưới ngưỡng nhận thức có ý thức; đừng nhầm với 'subtle' (tinh tế nhưng vẫn có thể nhận ra).
vocabulary.definition_en: perceived by or affecting the unconscious mind, without conscious awareness
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc tiềm thức, tác động ngầm (không nhận thức được)
vocabulary.example: Some advertising messages go into your brain without you even noticing, exploiting subliminal cues.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sub-' (dưới) + 'limen' (ngưỡng cửa, tiếng Latin) → thông điệp nằm dưới ngưỡng nhận thức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bão hoà, thị trường đã quá đầy một loại sản phẩm nên khó có thêm nhu cầu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The market being completely **saturated**, the company struggled to sell its new product.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Giống miếng bọt biển thấm no nước (saturated) → thị trường "ngấm no", không hấp thụ thêm được nữa.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng giới từ 'saturated WITH sth', không phải 'saturated BY sth', khi nói thị trường tràn ngập cái gì.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a market) so full of a particular type of product or content that little additional demand exists
vocabulary.definition_vi: bão hoà (thị trường, quá nhiều sản phẩm/nội dung tương tự)
vocabulary.example: The market being completely saturated, the company struggled to sell its new product.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Giống miếng bọt biển thấm no nước (saturated) → thị trường 'ngấm no', không hấp thụ thêm được nữa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự thao túng tâm lý hoặc hành vi của người khác một cách khéo léo, có chủ đích.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Advertisers often use psychological **manipulation** to convince consumers to buy products.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'manus' (bàn tay, Latin) → 'manipulate' = nắn bằng tay → khéo léo điều khiển người khác theo ý mình.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Manipulation' luôn mang hàm ý tiêu cực (thao túng có chủ đích); đừng dùng thay cho 'influence' (ảnh hưởng, trung tính).
vocabulary.definition_en: the act of skilfully or deceptively influencing someone's behaviour or beliefs to one's own advantage
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự thao túng (tâm lý, hành vi người khác)
vocabulary.example: Advertisers often use psychological manipulation to convince consumers to buy products.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'manus' (bàn tay, Latin) → 'manipulate' = nắn bằng tay → khéo léo điều khiển người khác theo ý mình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thông tin thiên lệch được lan truyền có chủ đích nhằm phục vụ mục đích chính trị.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The documentary was heavily biased, functioning almost as state **propaganda** for one political party.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin 'propagare' (nhân giống, lan truyền) → thông tin được "gieo trồng" và lan rộng để phục vụ mục đích chính trị.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Propaganda' là danh từ không đếm được, không viết 'a propaganda' hay 'propagandas'.
vocabulary.definition_en: information, especially biased or misleading, used to promote a particular political cause or point of view
vocabulary.definition_vi: tuyên truyền (thông tin thiên lệch nhằm mục đích chính trị)
vocabulary.example: The documentary was heavily biased, functioning almost as state propaganda for one political party.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Latin 'propagare' (nhân giống, lan truyền) → thông tin được 'gieo trồng' và lan rộng để phục vụ mục đích chính trị.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Lan tràn, hiện diện khắp nơi, thâm nhập vào mọi mặt của đời sống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The sheer saturation of advertising has rendered it a **pervasive**, inescapable feature of modern life.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'per-' (xuyên suốt) + 'vadere' (đi, Latin) → thấm lan đi khắp mọi ngóc ngách.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'pervasive' (lan tràn, ở khắp nơi) với 'persuasive' (có sức thuyết phục) - hai từ dễ đọc nhầm.
vocabulary.definition_en: spreading widely throughout an area or group of people; existing in every part of something
vocabulary.definition_vi: lan tràn, thâm nhập khắp nơi
vocabulary.example: The sheer saturation of advertising has rendered it a pervasive, inescapable feature of modern life.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'per-' (xuyên suốt) + 'vadere' (đi, Latin) → thấm lan đi khắp mọi ngóc ngách.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quyền tự do quyết định mua sắm của người tiêu dùng mà không bị chi phối quá mức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Critics argue that covert marketing tactics undermine **consumer autonomy** by manipulating decisions below the level of awareness.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'auto-' (tự) + 'nomos' (luật, Hy Lạp) → tự đặt luật cho chính mình → quyền tự quyết.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Autonomy' là danh từ trừu tượng không đếm được; tính từ tương ứng là 'autonomous', không phải 'autonomic' (thuộc hệ thần kinh tự trị).
vocabulary.definition_en: the freedom of consumers to make independent, rational purchasing decisions without undue external influence
vocabulary.definition_vi: quyền tự quyết của người tiêu dùng
vocabulary.example: Critics argue that covert marketing tactics undermine consumer autonomy by manipulating decisions below the level of awareness.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'auto-' (tự) + 'nomos' (luật, Hy Lạp) → tự đặt luật cho chính mình → quyền tự quyết.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thủ thuật thiết kế khiến người dùng cảm thấy xấu hổ hoặc áy náy nếu từ chối một lời đề nghị.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The user-experience researcher Harry Brignull catalogued dark patterns such as **confirmshaming**, where the decline button reads 'No thanks, I don't want to save money'.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
confirm (xác nhận) + shaming (làm xấu hổ) → khiến người dùng cảm thấy xấu hổ nếu từ chối xác nhận.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Confirmshaming' là thuật ngữ UX chuyên ngành (một loại dark pattern cụ thể), không viết tách rời thành 'confirm shaming'; luôn là danh từ không đếm được.
vocabulary.definition_en: a manipulative interface design that guilt-trips or shames a user into opting into something by phrasing the decline option negatively
vocabulary.definition_vi: thủ thuật gây xấu hổ để ép đồng ý (thiết kế khiến người dùng ngại từ chối)
vocabulary.example: The user-experience researcher Harry Brignull catalogued dark patterns such as confirmshaming, where the decline button reads 'No thanks, I don't want to save money'.
vocabulary.memory_hook: confirm (xác nhận) + shaming (làm xấu hổ) → khiến người dùng cảm thấy xấu hổ nếu từ chối xác nhận.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dần được chú ý và ủng hộ rộng rãi, tạo được đà lan rộng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Influencer marketing has **gained significant traction** among Gen Z, who trust peer recommendations over corporate advertising.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'traction' vốn nghĩa lực kéo bánh xe bám đường → một xu hướng "bám đường" và tăng tốc lan rộng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Traction' trong nghĩa bóng này không đếm được; tránh viết 'a traction' hay 'tractions'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to gradually gather momentum, popularity, or acceptance
vocabulary.definition_vi: dần được chú ý/ủng hộ rộng rãi, tạo được đà phát triển
vocabulary.example: Influencer marketing has gained significant traction among Gen Z, who trust peer recommendations over corporate advertising.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'traction' vốn nghĩa lực kéo bánh xe bám đường → một xu hướng 'bám đường' và tăng tốc lan rộng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thủ thuật giao diện khiến việc đăng ký dễ dàng nhưng việc huỷ bỏ dịch vụ lại vô cùng khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Familiar dark patterns include the **roach motel**, an interface that is easy to subscribe to but near-impossible to cancel.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
bẫy gián (roach motel) dễ vào nhưng gián không ra được → dịch vụ dễ đăng ký nhưng cực khó huỷ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Roach motel' là thuật ngữ ẩn dụ trong UX design (Harry Brignull, 2010), không dùng theo nghĩa đen 'nhà nghỉ có gián'; luôn đi kèm giải thích ngữ cảnh khi dùng lần đầu.
vocabulary.definition_en: a deceptive interface design that makes it easy to sign up for a service but extremely difficult to cancel or unsubscribe
vocabulary.definition_vi: thủ thuật 'dễ vào khó ra' (đăng ký dễ nhưng huỷ cực khó)
vocabulary.example: Familiar dark patterns include the roach motel, an interface that is easy to subscribe to but near-impossible to cancel.
vocabulary.memory_hook: bẫy gián (roach motel) dễ vào nhưng gián không ra được → dịch vụ dễ đăng ký nhưng cực khó huỷ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đạt được điều gì đó nhưng phải trả giá, gây tổn hại cho thứ khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Algorithms often prioritise sensationalism and clickbait headlines **at the expense of** factual, accurate reporting.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'expense' (chi phí) → làm điều gì đó phải trả một "cái giá" là tổn hại cho thứ khác.
vocabulary.common_error: Cấu trúc cố định 'at the expense of + noun/gerund', không chia động từ ngay sau 'of'.
vocabulary.definition_en: causing harm or loss to something else in the process of achieving a goal
vocabulary.definition_vi: phải trả giá bằng, gây tổn hại đến (cái gì khác)
vocabulary.example: Algorithms often prioritise sensationalism and clickbait headlines at the expense of factual, accurate reporting.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'expense' (chi phí) → làm điều gì đó phải trả một 'cái giá' là tổn hại cho thứ khác.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự lan truyền thông tin qua lời kể trực tiếp giữa người với người, không qua quảng cáo.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The local restaurant became incredibly famous purely through **word of mouth**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'word' (lời nói) + 'of mouth' (từ miệng) → thông tin truyền từ miệng người này sang người khác.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Word of mouth' là cụm danh từ không đếm được, thường đứng sau giới từ 'by/through', không thêm mạo từ 'a'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the passing of information or opinions from person to person by spoken communication rather than advertising
vocabulary.definition_vi: truyền miệng (lan truyền thông tin qua lời kể trực tiếp)
vocabulary.example: The local restaurant became incredibly famous purely through word of mouth.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'word' (lời nói) + 'of mouth' (từ miệng) → thông tin truyền từ miệng người này sang người khác.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trạng thái bị công chúng theo dõi, bàn tán và chú ý sát sao.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Growing up in the **public eye** can put immense psychological pressure on child actors.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'public' (công chúng) + 'eye' (con mắt) → luôn bị "con mắt" của công chúng dõi theo.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng với mạo từ xác định: 'in THE public eye', không bỏ 'the'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of being closely watched, known, and discussed by the general public
vocabulary.definition_vi: tầm mắt công chúng, sự chú ý của dư luận
vocabulary.example: Growing up in the public eye can put immense psychological pressure on child actors.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'public' (công chúng) + 'eye' (con mắt) → luôn bị 'con mắt' của công chúng dõi theo.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chuyên gia PR chuyên xoay chuyển thông tin theo hướng có lợi cho khách hàng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The company hired a professional **spin doctor** to manage the PR crisis after the scandal broke.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'spin' (xoay, vặn) một câu chuyện theo hướng có lợi → bác sĩ chuyên "chữa lành" hình ảnh xấu.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Spin' trong cụm này mang nghĩa bóng (lái/xoay chuyển thông tin), khác với nghĩa đen 'quay tròn'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a public relations expert employed to give a favourable interpretation of events, especially for a politician or public figure
vocabulary.definition_vi: chuyên gia PR chuyên 'lái' dư luận theo hướng có lợi
vocabulary.example: The company hired a professional spin doctor to manage the PR crisis after the scandal broke.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'spin' (xoay, vặn) một câu chuyện theo hướng có lợi → bác sĩ chuyên 'chữa lành' hình ảnh xấu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tin tức độc quyền mà một nhà báo hoặc tòa soạn công bố trước tất cả đối thủ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The ambitious reporter managed to get an **exclusive scoop** about the upcoming election.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'scoop' (múc lấy trước) → nhà báo "múc" được tin trước khi đối thủ kịp biết.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Scoop' trong ngữ cảnh báo chí là danh từ đếm được ('a scoop'), khác nghĩa đen 'cái muôi múc'.
vocabulary.definition_en: an important news story published by one journalist or news outlet before all others
vocabulary.definition_vi: tin độc quyền (đưa tin trước tất cả đối thủ)
vocabulary.example: The ambitious reporter managed to get an exclusive scoop about the upcoming election.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'scoop' (múc lấy trước) → nhà báo 'múc' được tin trước khi đối thủ kịp biết.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nhóm khách hàng hoặc khán giả cụ thể mà một chiến dịch quảng cáo nhắm tới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The campaign completely failed because it did not appeal to its **target audience**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'target' (mục tiêu, hình bia) + 'audience' (khán giả) → nhóm khán giả được nhắm bắn chính xác.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Target audience' là cụm danh từ ghép, không chia số nhiều thành 'audiences' trừ khi nói đến nhiều nhóm khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: the specific group of people that an advertisement, product, or campaign is designed to appeal to
vocabulary.definition_vi: đối tượng khách hàng/khán giả mục tiêu
vocabulary.example: The campaign completely failed because it did not appeal to its target audience.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'target' (mục tiêu, hình bia) + 'audience' (khán giả) → nhóm khán giả được nhắm bắn chính xác.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Việc thiết kế có chủ đích các giao diện số nhằm điều hướng hành vi người dùng vì mục đích thương mại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Digital interfaces are meticulously engineered as **persuasion architecture**, with every shade of colour A/B-tested to maximise time-on-platform.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'persuasion' (sự thuyết phục) + 'architecture' (kiến trúc) → giao diện được "xây" như một công trình để thuyết phục người dùng.
collocations: a textbook example of persuasion architecture
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là cụm danh từ học thuật cố định, không tách rời hoặc đảo ngược thành 'architecture of persuasion' khi trích dẫn thuật ngữ chuyên ngành.
vocabulary.definition_en: the deliberate design of digital interfaces and environments to nudge and shape user behaviour, typically for commercial ends
vocabulary.definition_vi: kiến trúc thuyết phục (thiết kế giao diện số nhằm điều hướng hành vi người dùng)
vocabulary.example: Digital interfaces are meticulously engineered as persuasion architecture, with every shade of colour A/B-tested to maximise time-on-platform.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'persuasion' (sự thuyết phục) + 'architecture' (kiến trúc) → giao diện được 'xây' như một công trình để thuyết phục người dùng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Các thủ thuật thiết kế giao diện nhằm đánh lừa hoặc ép buộc người dùng hành động ngoài ý muốn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A 2022 audit by the European Commission found **dark patterns** on ninety-seven percent of the major e-commerce sites surveyed.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'dark' (đen tối, giấu giếm) + 'pattern' (khuôn mẫu thiết kế) → những khuôn mẫu thiết kế "đen tối" nhằm gài bẫy người dùng.
vocabulary.common_error: Thuật ngữ luôn ở dạng số nhiều 'dark patterns' khi chỉ chung hiện tượng thiết kế, dù nói về một kỹ thuật cụ thể vẫn thường giữ số nhiều trong văn phong học thuật.
vocabulary.definition_en: interface designs deliberately crafted to deceive, mislead, or coerce users into actions they would not otherwise choose
vocabulary.definition_vi: thủ thuật giao diện lừa dối (thiết kế đánh lừa người dùng)
vocabulary.example: A 2022 audit by the European Commission found dark patterns on ninety-seven percent of the major e-commerce sites surveyed.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'dark' (đen tối, giấu giếm) + 'pattern' (khuôn mẫu thiết kế) → những khuôn mẫu thiết kế 'đen tối' nhằm gài bẫy người dùng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mô hình kinh tế trong đó sự chú ý của con người trở thành nguồn tài nguyên khan hiếm, được các nền tảng cạnh tranh khai thác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> In the **attention economy**, modern media companies don't sell products; they sell user attention to advertisers.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'attention' (sự chú ý) trở thành hàng hoá trong 'economy' (nền kinh tế) → càng giữ được chú ý càng kiếm được tiền.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'attention economy' (mô hình kinh tế học) với 'economy' đơn thuần nghĩa 'nền kinh tế quốc gia'.
vocabulary.definition_en: an economic model in which human attention is treated as a scarce, monetisable resource that platforms compete to capture
vocabulary.definition_vi: nền kinh tế chú ý (sự chú ý của con người trở thành nguồn tài nguyên được kinh doanh)
vocabulary.example: In the attention economy, modern media companies don't sell products; they sell user attention to advertisers.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'attention' (sự chú ý) trở thành hàng hoá trong 'economy' (nền kinh tế) → càng giữ được chú ý càng kiếm được tiền.
